source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Food and Nutrition past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A woman who sells fried plantain and avocado salad at a school gate slices her fruit early in the morning. By midday the slices have turned brown and fewer pupils want to buy them. The same sort of change makes bananas soften and tomatoes spoil in the heat. Chemical changes caused by enzymes explain much of this, and the GCE asks you to name those changes, to describe them briefly and to tell enzymes apart from the pigments that give vegetables their colours.

items: Proteins are made of amino acids and are changed by heat.
Micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) are living things that can spoil food.
Fruits and vegetables contain vitamin C, which is easily lost.

sections.titre: Enzymes, the spoilage they cause and how it is controlled
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What enzymes are
Enzymes are protein substances, made by living cells, that speed up chemical reactions without being used up (biological catalysts). They are present in raw plant and animal foods. Each enzyme acts on one kind of substance. Enzymes are not living organisms.

| Condition | Effect on enzymes |
|---|---|
| Cold (refrigerator, freezer) | work very slowly or not at all, but are not destroyed |
| Warmth | work fastest |
| High temperature, as in boiling or blanching | destroyed for good |
| Strong acid | slows or stops many of them |

### Spoilage caused by enzymes
| Action | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Enzymic browning | cut banana, apple, avocado or potato | the cut surface turns brown and looks unattractive |
| Over-ripening | banana, mango, pawpaw, tomato | the fruit becomes too soft and sweet and moulds attack it |
| Loss of vitamin C | vegetables cut and left standing | enzymes help to destroy the vitamin |
| Breakdown of fat | stored nuts and fats | fat is split into fatty acids and glycerol, giving a rancid smell and taste |
| Breakdown of meat and fish after slaughter | meat and fish left warm | flesh softens, so bacteria enter more easily |

### Controlling enzyme action
Cooking and blanching (brief scalding of vegetables before freezing) destroy enzymes; refrigeration and freezing slow them; lemon juice or other acids slow browning; covering cut fruit with water or sugar syrup keeps air away; salting and drying also help.

### Useful enzymes
Enzymes in yeast ferment sugar to make bread rise, an enzyme in the stomach of young animals clots milk in cheese making, and papain from pawpaw tenderises meat.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks about the colours of fruit and vegetables or how cooking changes them.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Pigments are coloured substances, not enzymes.

| Pigment | Colour and example | Effect of cooking |
|---|---|---|
| Chlorophyll | green, as in spinach | acid turns it olive-brown; alkali keeps it bright but destroys vitamin C and softens the vegetable |
| Carotene | orange or yellow, as in carrot and red palm oil | not changed by acid or alkali; dissolves in fat; the body can change it into vitamin A |
| Xanthophyll | yellow, related to carotene | stable in cooking |
| Anthocyanin | red, purple or blue, as in red cabbage | dissolves in water; stays red in acid and turns bluish in alkali |
| Anthoxanthins | white, cream or pale yellow, as in cauliflower, potato and onion | stay white in acid and turn yellow in alkali; quercetin belongs to this group |

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to list and describe actions of enzymes that spoil food.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For each action write its name, one sentence of description with an example, and the result. Choose three different actions, for example enzymic browning, over-ripening and rancidity. Two marks per action: one for the name and one for the description.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to compare causes of food spoilage.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Enzymes are chemical substances inside the food itself, but micro-organisms are living things that come from outside. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds need food, moisture, warmth and time to grow. Heat kills them, cold and drying stop them from multiplying, and acids, sugar and salt hold them back.

sections.enonce_markdown: A girl slices ripe bananas for a fruit salad and leaves them in the open air for two hours. The slices turn brown. (a) Name the change that has taken place. (b) Explain why it occurs. (c) State three ways of preventing it. (d) Why does cooking the bananas stop the change? (6 marks)

etapes.justification: Browning of a cut fruit by an enzyme is called enzymic browning.
Cutting breaks cells, so an enzyme in the fruit meets other substances in the fruit and oxygen from the air; they react to form brown substances.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Enzyme + substances in the fruit + oxygen from the air give brown colour.

etapes.justification: Each measure stops the enzyme or keeps air away.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Sprinkle with lemon juice; cover with water or syrup; serve soon after cutting.

etapes.action: Explain why heat stops the change.
etapes.justification: An enzyme is a protein, and high temperature destroys it.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Cooking destroys the enzyme, so browning cannot occur.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** Enzymic browning. **(b)** When the fruit is cut, an enzyme in the fruit reacts with substances in it and with oxygen from the air to form brown substances. **(c)** Sprinkle the slices with lemon juice; cover them with water or sugar syrup; prepare them just before serving. **(d)** The enzyme is a protein and heat destroys it, so no browning can occur.

items.erreur_markdown: 'Enzymes are tiny living organisms like bacteria.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Enzymes are protein substances made by cells; they are not alive and do not multiply.
items.correction_markdown: Enzymes are biological catalysts; bacteria, yeasts and moulds are the living organisms.

items.pourquoi_faux: Cold only slows or stops them; they work again when the food thaws. Heat destroys them, which is why vegetables are blanched before freezing.
items.correction_markdown: Freezing slows enzyme action; blanching or cooking destroys enzymes.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that carotene, anthocyanin or xanthophyll are enzymes.
items.pourquoi_faux: These are pigments, coloured substances that give colour to vegetables and fruits.
items.correction_markdown: Name the enzyme action and the pigment separately: enzymes cause changes, pigments give colour.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that a cut apple turns brown because bacteria have attacked it.
items.pourquoi_faux: The change is quick and is caused by an enzyme acting with oxygen. Bacteria need time to grow.
items.correction_markdown: State enzymic browning, caused by an enzyme and oxygen.

items.erreur_markdown: Naming an action such as 'lipase acts on fat' without saying what the result is.
items.pourquoi_faux: The mark scheme asks for the spoilage that follows.
items.correction_markdown: Add: the fat is split into fatty acids and glycerol and the food becomes rancid.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) What is an enzyme? (b) Give two ways of making enzymes in food inactive or destroying them. (c) Name one fruit that turns brown when it is cut.
items.solution_markdown: (a) An enzyme is a protein substance, made by living cells, that speeds up a chemical reaction. (b) Any two: **cooking or blanching with heat; keeping food in the refrigerator or freezer (slows them); adding lemon juice or another acid**. (c) **Banana** (also apple, avocado or potato).

items.enonce_markdown: Name the pigment responsible for each colour: (a) the orange of carrot; (b) the green of spinach; (c) the red of red cabbage; (d) the cream of cauliflower. (e) State what happens to red cabbage when vinegar is added.
items.solution_markdown: (a) **Carotene**. (b) **Chlorophyll**. (c) **Anthocyanin**. (d) **Anthoxanthin**. (e) Acid makes it stay a bright **red**; alkali turns it bluish.

items.enonce_markdown: A trader buys 50 kg of ripe tomatoes at 350 FCFA per kilogram (assumed price). After two hot days, 20% of them are too soft to sell. (a) Calculate the cost of the tomatoes. (b) Find the mass of tomatoes spoilt and the mass left to sell. (c) Calculate the money spent on the spoilt tomatoes. (d) Explain two ways in which enzymes and micro-organisms cause this loss. (e) Suggest two ways of reducing the loss.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $50 \times 350 = 17\,500$, so **17,500 FCFA**. (b) $\dfrac{20}{100} \times 50 = 10$ kg spoilt, so **10 kg spoilt and 40 kg left**. (c) $10 \times 350 = 3\,500$, so **3,500 FCFA**. (d) Enzymes in the ripe fruit keep softening it, which makes it over-ripe and easy to bruise; moulds and bacteria then grow on the soft fruit and rot it. (e) Any two: keep the tomatoes in a cool, shaded, airy place; buy fruit that is less ripe; sort out and sell soft ones quickly; process surplus tomatoes into paste or dry them.

items_markdown: Enzymes are protein catalysts present in raw foods. They are destroyed by heat, slowed by cold and are not living things.
Spoilage by enzymes: enzymic browning, over-ripening, loss of vitamin C, rancidity of fats and softening of meat and fish after slaughter.
Control: cooking and blanching destroy enzymes; cold slows them; acids such as lemon juice and the exclusion of air reduce browning.
Pigments (chlorophyll, carotene, xanthophyll, anthocyanin and anthoxanthins) give colour; they are not enzymes.
In 'describe briefly' questions, give three different actions, each with a name, a description with an example and the result on the food.
